item.title: The Two Devils of PTZ Cameras: Long-Focus Amplification and Dead Time
item.description:
If you’ve used a security PTZ dome long enough, you’ve probably seen these symptoms:

  • Rock-steady at wide angle, but a persistent jitter once you zoom into telephoto.
  • Preset recall is spot-on at wide angle, but off by half a screen at telephoto.
  • Joystick control always feels “half a beat behind” — you push, wait for the frame to change, but by the time it does, the gimbal has already overshot. So you correct, overshoot again, oscillate.
  • AI auto-tracking works fine at wide angle, but the target starts swinging left-right once you zoom in.

Same camera — why is it fine at wide angle and broken at telephoto? Why is joystick control never precise?

item.title: PTZ Latency End-to-End: From Encoding to Transport Optimization
item.description:
The operator calls: the PTZ feed is several seconds behind. Push the joystick and the far end reacts long after. Ops swaps the camera first—no change; suspects the network—RTT measured, normal; finally shrinks the player buffer—the problem disappears on the spot.

That is not a skit; it is the standard path of a “latency complaint”: swap hardware first, check the network second, and only then get to the real problem. The previous post in this series, “The Two Devils of PTZ Cameras,” named latency one of the two devils. This one tears it apart: where each millisecond goes, what can be optimized, and what is a hard protocol limitation.
